content.thinking:
I'm designing the kitsune as a large fantasy fox with nine tails fanned out behind it, each glowing with floating spirit flames rendered as translucent blue-violet flame shapes for an otherworldly effect.

I'm working out the skeleton coordinates carefully since I can't typecheck anything—defining hips, spine chain, and neck positions in world space using explicit coordinate conventions so the body curves naturally from hips through chest to a slightly lowered head.

For the joint hierarchy, I'll set a root "pelvis" joint at the hips position, then build the spine chain as a child, letting the first spine joint overlap with the pelvis location since that's harmless. I'm also planning the tail as nine chains radiating from the rump, each with four joints, alongside four-legged limbs with four joints apiece, plus neck, head, jaw, ears, and whisker joints to round out the full skeleton.

Flames and other decorative elements don't need their own joints since they'll just bind to the nearest skeletal joint automatically, which works fine for things hovering near the tail tips. For the tail fan itself, I'm working out the arrangement so the nine tails spread in an arc behind the body like a peacock fan, with each tail's angle distributed across roughly a 150-degree spread centered upward, and I'm defining the path each tail takes outward from that angle.

Each tail curves back and out from its root, with the spread kept within safe bounds so even the sideways-most tails stay clear of the ground given their fluffy radius. I want to add some droop at the tips for a more natural curl, and vary the lengths so the center tail is longest while the outer ones taper shorter.

For color, I'm settling on a cream-white kitsune coat with crimson kumadori-style markings and gold accents, tails fading from cream into a blue-violet spirit-flame tip for that elegant high-fantasy look.

Still writing gradient/cel logic...

For fur, I'm thinking about using furEdge for the belly transition and considering the body's overall coloring—mostly cream white like a classic kitsune with possible red saddle markings on the back.

Now I'm designing the markings: crimson kumadori face lines, dark plum socks on the legs gradient toward the paws like black fox feet, plum ear backs with cream interior, and red flame-tipped tails. For decoration, I'm adding a gold collar with bell and tassel, a crescent moon forehead ornament, and a red-and-gold ceremonial rope around the neck.

I'm also working out gold cuff bands near the base of each tail, computing the tail radius at that point so the bands fit snugly, then sweeping closed ring geometry along each tail to form the bracelet-like effect across all nine tails.

Now I'm thinking through fur texture for the mane, chest ruff, cheeks, and tail tips — using light cream and grey-shaded tuft drawings so color tinting applies correctly, even though these fur cards won't be cel-shaded like the rest of the body.

For the flames (hitodama), I'm designing a teardrop texture with layered colors — violet-blue outer, cyan middle, white core — rendered as glowing cross-cards standing upright via frame orientation. I'm planning around 14 floating flames plus extras attached at each tail tip to look like they're burning there.

Each hitodama will have a small glowing sphere core topped with a glowing flame card, keeping floating flames above floor level so none clip into the ground.

Now I'm planning the body construction, defining a spine chain with points running from pelvis through chest, and a separate neck chain connecting to the head base.

I'll simplify by treating the torso as one continuous sweep using a single bone chain of pelvis, spine, and neck, with the path running rump to chest to neck base to head base, letting each joint claim the path segment where it projects.

Still defining skeleton joints...

I'm sketching the fox skull as an ellipsoid with a tapered snout sweep toward the nose, defining the upper and lower jaw bones with separate radius profiles, and placing a dark nose sphere at the tip with a cream-colored lower jaw.

I'm adding tiny white fang cones at the mouth corners for a stylized fox look, then setting up two-bone chains for big pointed ears, defining base and mid joint positions to shape their curve upward.

Still writing ear outline geometry...

Checking convexity of the ear polygon by computing cross products of consecutive edge vectors to confirm all turns go the same direction.

For the ear tilt, I'm experimenting with the x and y directions for the leaning effect, noting the docs' mirror example uses a slightly different non-orthogonal setup than what I'm trying.

Working out the thickness normal direction for both bone orientations, I confirm it faces properly either way. Now I'm placing the extrude at the ear base bone joint, and setting up a smaller cream/pink inner-ear outline offset slightly forward on the ear's front-facing side.

For coloring, I'm giving the ear a dark plum base paint, then using a custom paint function so the outer ear tip transitions to dark plum via a gradient oriented mostly along the Y axis.

Now I'm placing the eyes as decals on the skull surface, choosing a golden amber iris for a kitsune look, positioned symmetrically at an azimuth around 38 degrees to sit naturally on the sides of the fox face.

I'm also planning red kumadori-style markings as flat swoosh decals extending from the eye corners back toward the ears, giving that stylized anime warrior-mask accent.

I'll place the swoosh marking above-back of the eye and a second cheek line below, both red, plus a forehead decal like a red teardrop or gold crescent ornament positioned at the top.

Writing torus geometry parameters...

Positioning the torus so it faces outward from the skull's surface normal at that forehead point, orienting its axis along the hit direction with a small offset to keep it from clipping into the mesh.

I'm also adding a tiny red-orange gem sphere glowing in front of the crescent, and writing a helper to safely unwrap nullable hit results since `.at()` can return null. For the head bone, I'm attaching the skull geometry and pose directly to it.

Now I'm working out the torso's shape by sweeping radius values along the body path from rump to neck, tuning an array of radii keyed roughly to position even though the knot spacing isn't perfectly even—good enough for a believable silhouette.

I realize I should just reuse the `b.loft` helper with station points and bone references for the pelvis-spine-neck chain, matching the same interpolation approach used elsewhere, rather than reinventing the radius function.

Now I'm sketching out the actual station coordinates and widths/heights along the torso -- from rump through hips, waist, chest, and up toward the shoulders -- adjusting the ellipse dimensions at each point to get a believable body profile, and checking how the belly depth relates to leg length below.

With legs scaled from the hips, I'm settling on a tall, elegant fox around 1.7m at full tail/ear height -- plausible for a large spirit-fox design. I'm planning the spine loft through pelvis, spine, and neck joints via a catmull path, then thinking through the fur shading: cream on the back with a paler, slightly warmer belly tone handled by cel shading, plus a furEdge detail marking the flank boundary between the two colors.

I'm now considering decorative red markings -- maybe kumadori-style brush-stroke stripes across the back and haunches, or a dorsal ridge stripe with a zigzag edge based on noise functions along the spine, going for something tasteful rather than overdone.

Then I pivot toward a tomoe-like ring mark on the thighs: computing distance from a haunch-center point in 3D and painting a red ring band with cream inside and a small inner dot accent, placed symmetrically on both hips.

Working out mark placement...

Also planning the shoulder mark placement, then moving to leg geometry: slender digitigrade hind legs and front legs built from shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw segments with specified lengths and bend directions for the limb function.

For the hind leg I'm using a three-segment limb so the knee bends forward and the hock bends back, giving that digitigrade stance, with joint names running from hip through knee and hock down to the ankle.

I'm placing the paw sphere so its lowest point sits right at ground level, adjusting the center height and radius to roughly 0.032 so it just touches the floor without sinking noticeably.

For the legs, I'm applying a gradient paint so the cream fur transitions into a dark plum "stocking" color higher up the leg, mimicking the look of socks like on black foxes. I'm also adding a thin gold torus ring around each ankle, rotated flat to wrap horizontally around the leg.

Using `at: cp` directly since it's a frame, with the tangent vector as the direction. For the leg's gold rings, I'll scale the torus radius down to about 0.04 to match the tube's taper near t=0.8, using a low-poly torus for the flat gold look. Then I move on to planning the nine tails.

Each tail chain gets 5 joints, bringing the total joint count to 71 once I add pelvis, spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, and legs. The tail root attaches to the pelvis joint, and I'm naming each segment with sequential suffixes like tail1a through tail1e to keep valid identifier names while representing a 5-point catmull chain per tail.

Now I'm working out the fan geometry for the nine tails, spacing their angles evenly from -68° to 68° and computing each root point's position so they sweep back and curve upward and outward.

I'm checking whether the tails overlap too much given their angular spacing and radius, and deciding to cap the outer radius and widen the fan angle to about ±72° with 18° steps to keep the fluffy look without excessive clumping.

Computing tail positions with alternating z offsets for interleaving, plus upward curl on the outer tails for a more elegant arc...

I realize the tail height is overshooting the fox's total 2m frame, so I need to shrink the shoulder-to-tail length and tilt the fan axis backward rather than straight up, giving the tails a swept-back, upward-angled spread instead of towering too tall.

Let me try a vertical fan arrangement instead, like a peacock behind the fox, with the plane perpendicular to the forward axis so the tails curve up and outward—targeting a tallest tip around 1.5 units high with the center tail arcing back and up.

Still computing tail geometry...

Still writing tail geometry... checking that the center tail's tip lands around y=1.58, consistent with the model's overall height near 1.6.

Now I'm setting the tail radius profile along its length, giving it a plump, fluffy middle that tapers to a rounded tip, with outer tails scaled slightly narrower than the center one.

For color, I'm deciding on a cream-to-crimson gradient along each tail with glowing cyan flame accents at the tip, kept consistent across all nine tails rather than varying per-tail, plus a fur-edge zigzag technique to blend the cream and red sections along the tail's length.

Still defining fur edge parameters...

For the gold tail rings, I'm checking spacing against the tail radius since multiple tails overlap near the root, and finding the rings will mostly overlap but that's acceptable visually since the overlapping bits get hidden anyway.

Still planning the ring sweep geometry...

Instead of a tassel on every ring I'll put one gold pendant at the neck. Checking budget: parts and triangle counts stay well under limits even with nine tail sweeps and chain joints, and I'm scattering fur cards across the chest and neck using a filtered surface scatter.

Scattering more fur cards on the cheeks and sparse tufts near the tail tip...

For sideways tails, direction relative to the surface is arbitrary but consistent, so a better flow would point toward the tail tip using the tangent at the path's end, letting the tuft lean into the tip direction while flattened onto the surface. For filtering scatter hits past the midpoint, I can check closestT against the path rather than relying on unknown t-values, and I'll derive the tail surface from the sweep itself via `b.surface(tailSweep)`.

Now I'm sketching the head: placing the skull as a scaled sphere at the head joint, painting it cream, then defining the snout as a tapering sweep from the face toward a nose tip with a radius function that shrinks along the path.

Still placing nose geometry...

Then I move to the lower jaw, sweeping a tapered radius path from the chin forward to form the jawline.

Adding lip line details...

Then I'm planning the whiskers: three thin tapered sweeps per side running from the muzzle outward and slightly back, using tapering radii to create a natural whisker shape.

For eyes, I'm sizing the decal based on skull proportions, positioning them symmetrically with azimuth and elevation offsets to sit correctly on the face, with eyelid brow details folded into the same decal.

For the red kumadori streaks, I'm using filled SVG paths rather than thin strokes for robustness, placing these decals symmetrically across the face.

Now I'm working through the orientation math for each side's decal — figuring out which direction the drawing's horizontal axis should face based on viewer perspective and up-vector, so the swoosh shape reads correctly (front-to-back) whether mirrored for the left or right side.

With the mirror logic settled, I'm moving on to the forehead marking — sketching a teardrop/diamond shape pointing downward for a decal.

For positioning, the decal at elevation 62° tilts enough that the drawing's "up" direction ends up angled backward-up, which conveniently means the teardrop's point naturally aims forward-down toward the nose. I'll size it [0.035, 0.055] and may need to nudge the gold crescent down to elevation 38° to avoid overlap.

I'm checking the skull geometry more carefully: placing the crescent around elevation 52° and the teardrop lower, around elevation 24° at azimuth 0, right where the skull transitions into the snout. Working through the z-coordinates confirms the teardrop at that elevation still sits cleanly on the skull surface rather than spilling onto the snout.

I'm now checking eye placement at azimuth 40° on the skull, verifying that the x/z coordinates land near the snout's base on either side, but I notice the snout geometry would partially overlap and hide the inner portion of each eye decal since the snout's radius at that height covers part of the eye's x-range.

Since the eyes are getting buried inside the snout tube, I'm adjusting the angles outward and upward—trying azimuth 50°, elevation 12°—and recalculating the resulting point to see if it clears the snout's surface boundary at that z-depth.

Checking the snout start position against the skull's front curvature, the emergence point around z=0.84 has a small half-width there, so the snout barely overlaps the eye region at that depth. That settles the geometry reasonably well.

Now I'm adding cheek fur: small spike-shaped cones per side that flare backward and outward to give that classic fox cheek silhouette, using a few layered spikes with flat bases hidden inside the skull.

For the neck, I'm wrapping a red shimenawa-style rope around the neck area, computing a loop point and tangent direction along the throat so the sweep follows the neck curve naturally, then adding gold knots and paper tassel details to the rope.

Now I'm figuring out the shide paper strips — zigzag white cards hanging from the rope, selecting frame points along the front half of the loop path to hang about five cards facing downward and outward.

I'll write the callback to simply collect each point into an array rather than worry about its exact return type, since void works fine regardless.

Now for the gold bell placement, I'm figuring out where the front of the neck loop sits in 3D space—trying to locate the surface point near the neck front by estimating from the neck's center and radius rather than relying on a ray query.

I'll attach the bell sphere there with gold material, then add hanging tassels with red cords plus a gold disc accent. I'm mindful of keeping the file manageable in length and being careful with unused variables since TypeScript strictness will flag them, though I can't verify this until later.

For the glowing elements, I'll use cards with a glow effect for the flame texture. Then I'm placing a scattered ring of floating hitodama orbs at varying heights and radii around the fox and its tails, with a few smaller ones near the paws for grounding.

Each spirit-flame orb pairs a tiny pale sphere core with layered flame cards above it, slightly offset in angle for depth, both glowing. For the tail tip, I want a larger flame standing upright, oriented along the tail's outward direction at its endpoint.

Positioning the tip flame just beyond the tail's rounded end with a slight outward lean, giving it a flow direction based on the tangent angle so it reads as emerging naturally from the tip.

Skipping the spirit sparks idea, I shift to the gold ear ornaments instead, adding small torus rings with tassel cords near the ear base, working out the x-offsets so each ear's decoration centers correctly along the head's width.

Still working out sash geometry...

Now thinking about sash tails hanging from the knot, planning a flowing ribbon down the flank using a swept box section with a curved path, though the orientation of the ribbon's cross-section is still uncertain.

Defining ribbon outline points...

Now I'm thinking about toes and claws for the paws — adding three small cream-plum spheres per paw front for toe bumps instead of bothering with claw cones, keeping it minimal. I also need to plan the chest ruff and thigh fur cards, then figure out how to bone the ears, maybe using a simple chain without a strict role since nothing quite fits.

For the ears I'll just name the joints uniquely per side so they don't collide with other names, and the tail will parent off the pelvis with a smooth sweeping chain built from a catmull curve through an array of points. I'm working out how the chain function takes that path and sweeps geometry along it, making sure the gradient and joint spacing follow the curve correctly, then defining cream and darker cream color pairs for the fur paint.

Now I'm defining the rest of the color palette—red, plum, and gold tones—deciding between flat colors and cel-shaded paint pairs for the gold parts to keep the palette under the flat-color limit while still getting consistent anime-style shading, then thinking through how paint applies to sphere and torus geometries before moving on to eye details like iris and blush colors.

Writing the body paint logic...

Still placing marking positions...

For paint, the head stays plain cream while the body loft uses the same paint across neck and chest since markings apply spatially rather than by part. For legs I'm setting up a gradient from cream to plum along a vertical span to shade the limb.

Writing leg paint function...

I'm adding a zigzag toothed edge to the sock boundary so the plum color meets cream in a jagged cel-shaded line, plus a gold anklet torus ring above it, and defining a separate plum paint for the paws.

Now I'm working through the hind leg's inverse kinematics, placing hip and foot targets and choosing segment lengths and bend directions for a 3-joint limb chain, checking whether the last segment can run vertically parallel to the root-to-target line given the reach constraints.

For the front leg, I'm setting shoulder and target positions with a simpler two-segment chain that's nearly straight, considering whether to add a wrist/pastern joint for a more digitigrade look, and naming the chain points (shoulder, elbow, wrist) for the front limb role.

Now I'm working out tapering radius arrays for both legs: thinner for the front leg (around 0.062 down to 0.03) since it fits inside the chest width, and bulkier for the hind thigh (starting near 0.085) to give it a more muscular shape at the hip.

I'm also adding a haunch bulge using a scaled sphere at the thigh, positioned relative to the hip joint, and figuring out how to color and sweep the leg geometry with rounded caps. For attaching paws, I need to grab the final joint in the leg chain rather than relying on a typed `tip` property since that could be null.

Now I'm setting up the jaw joint under the head, then adding fangs as small flat-white cones positioned near the snout, working out their base position and length so they sit naturally against the snout's curve at that z-depth.

I decide to only use upper fangs since the lower jaw geometry would make lower fangs overlap awkwardly. Then I move to cheek tufts, planning spikes attached to the head bone with cream coloring, stacking a few per side with slight variation for a natural tufted look before moving on to the ear and whiskers.

Skipping eyebrows, I'm adding cream forelock cards scattered on top of the skull between the ears for a soft hair tuft, and considering a fur ruff around the torso using scattered surface cards filtered to the lower neck/chest area. I'm also toying with adding a faint ghostly flame-like mane along the spine from neck to tail for a spirit-creature effect.

Writing flame frame code...

Adding flame layers...

Now I'm thinking about creating a paper texture for the shide zigzag strips, using a white fill with light grey fold lines to suggest paper folds at this small size.

Still writing fur tuft shapes...

I want to make sure the neck chain and spine loft share consistent joint positions, so I'm defining a single set of coordinate points (A through F) for pelvis, spine, and neck to reuse across both the skeleton and the sweep, with the head joint anchored at F.

Now I'm checking how the head joint at F aligns toward the skull center and nose tip, figuring out a small downward-tilted aim vector so the head bone points naturally into the face rather than straight ahead. I'm also verifying the neck loft's radius tapers correctly so the neck mesh tucks under the skull without gaps, checking that the skull's bottom sits just above where the neck station ends.

I shift focus to the jaw joint, parenting it under the head and aiming it slightly downward toward the mouth, then confirm the rest pose stays neutral with no extra rotation applied. Looking at the torso stations, I adjust the rump cap position so the tail root hides inside it rather than poking through, nudging the tail's starting radius point from -0.58 to -0.54 so it emerges cleanly from the rump's rounded end cap while still being parented to the pelvis.

Writing tail chain code...

I verify the outer tail positions by checking the angle math: at 70 degrees the tip lands around y=1.05, x=0.77, z=-0.86, which curves nicely outward and upward. The center tail stretches further, with its tip reaching about y=1.5 and z=-1.06, giving a believable upward-backward sweep, and the first segment's direction from the root looks correctly aimed for a natural joint bend.

I'm defining tail radius profiles that taper from thin at the base to wide in the middle and narrow again at the tip, then setting up fur coloring along each tail using its tangent direction and a position-based level so the coat pattern follows the tail's orientation rather than a fixed axis -- though I need to account for the fact that tails point sideways rather than along the default axis.

For the gold accent rings around each tail, I'm considering sweeping a ring of points through a catmull curve at a fixed radius offset from the tail's cross-section, using the tail bone's rigidity to keep the ring aligned correctly.

For the tail, I'm thinking flames plus orbs plus spine pieces, each as separate mesh calls. Tallying up the part count: torso, four leg sweeps with haunches and paws, and so on.

Still adding paw details, toes, and claw cones, keeping the total part count under control while adding small spike details for each paw.

Claws get an ivory tone instead of ink, and I'm checking the sphere scaling so the paw, toes, and claws all sit flush with the floor without clipping below ground level.

The leg tube endpoints and paw sphere placement line up consistently so the foot geometry reads naturally, and the thin tube radius relative to the wider paw still looks fine once painted. Comparing head size to body proportions, the fox looks appropriately cute, and using a generic Part for eye decal surfaces should work fine.

I'm scattering gold crescent decals across the skull surface using hit-based positioning and orientation, aiming each crescent's axis along the surface normal so it opens upward correctly.

Still rotating the torus geometry...

Then I'm adding a glowing red gem sphere positioned at the center of each crescent's opening.

I need to import THREE properly and set up a type-safe helper for validating surface hits, making sure the generic syntax works in a .ts file. I'm also checking how the decal function signature handles hit-based positioning for the eye decal.

Now I'm designing the swoosh marking as an SVG path with curved red shapes, then placing it on the skull using azimuth and elevation coordinates near the eye-to-cheek area.

I need to check for overlap between the eye decal and swoosh placement -- the eye's angular span on the skull circumference reaches roughly 34-66° azimuth, so I'm adjusting the swoosh to start around 68° to avoid collision.

Checking the skull's widest point against the swoosh placement, I realize it's mostly hidden from a front view but visible from three-quarters. I'll also add small tear-mark stripes below the eye using a curved SVG path for a subtle facial detail.

Actually, the eye overlaps the blush area and the snout region interferes with lower placement, so I'll skip the cheek stripes and keep just the swoosh plus a forehead teardrop mark. A more robust alternative would be drawing the kumadori lines as draped sweeps directly on the skull surface with tapering, rather than flat decals.

Adding more facial marking sweeps...

For the neck, I'm building a rope loop as a closed path swept along the torso surface, colored red with a thinner gold rope offset slightly beside it.

For the shide, I'm filtering the rope's frame points to the lower front section, then placing small hanging card shapes at those points facing upward with a slight lean, getting around five or six cards total.

For the bell, I'm casting a hit from the neck point downward-forward to find the surface, then attaching a small gold sphere there embedded slightly with a ring and a dark slit detail.

I'm also adding a hanging tassel: a red rod extending down from the bell's hit point, capped with a spike fringe for texture.

I'm placing sash loops around the torso in red and gold at different depths, then planning decorative ribbons with a gold knot sphere at the side.

Checking the extrusion direction setup for the ribbons isn't constant along y, then adjusting tilt and position so ribbons sit correctly against the torso's width at that height.

Placing the gold ribbon at z=-0.16 so it clears the hind thigh, and positioning a dorsal spirit-flame mane along the torso curve using a set of frame points spaced from the neck down the back.

Checking off the detail list — eyes, markings, fur cards, claws, accessories, spirit flames, and inner ears are all covered, and I decide the fox doesn't need gold tail-tip caps after all.

I think a glowing magic circle decal on the floor beneath the fox would add a nice storytelling touch — a thin textured plane facing upward with rune-like markings in cyan and violet, sized to stay within the model's bounds and visible from a top-down camera angle.

Using 1024 texture size for the atlas, and sizing the decal plane around 2.2 m to fit the creature's footprint with fanned tails, with alpha cutout so transparent pixels don't render. Now I'm setting up the imports for the builder, frame, math helpers, IK limb logic, path utilities, and paint/gradient tools to start writing the actual generation code.

Importing the sweep radius function, texture utilities, toon shading kit (eye, cel shading, fur edges, zigzag, ink lines), and glow kit, then confirming each import maps to a specific use case like whisker lines using INK and ears using polyline. I'm defining the metadata object for the nine-tailed kitsune build, then starting the build function with a seeded random generator and thinking through where to place the color palette definition.

Now I'm defining the joint positions for the spine chain (pelvis through upper spine) and setting up the pelvis as the root joint with a spine role, then chaining the spine joints using catmull-rom interpolation between the points. I'm working out how to attach the neck chain to the last spine joint, reasoning through the point count and span relationships to make sure the neck segments connect correctly to the head position.

Confirming neck1 lands at spine3's endpoint, then adding the head joint parented to neck2 with an aim direction, followed by a jaw joint attached to the head. I'm also writing symmetric ear chains for left and right sides using polyline paths with three points each, parented to the head, and thinking through how the ear's local x-axis should point outward based on sign.

The ear shape has an asymmetric outline that tilts outward as it rises, and I'm working out how the base offset plus tilt pushes the tip's world-space x-coordinate further outside the head.

I should dial back the outward tilt angle to something more subtle, around 12 degrees instead of 14, and verify the ear base position emerges correctly from the skull's curved surface at that height.

Now I'm defining the inner ear shape, a small pink pointed polygon positioned just inside the outer ear outline with a slightly darker shade for depth, and checking that the points form a convex, non-self-intersecting shape.

Computing the cross products confirms the thickness axis points +z for one side and -z for the other, with the extrusion centered symmetrically so both ear sides get equal offset placement.

Now I'm setting up the ear color gradient, transitioning from cream to plum around y=1.2 to 1.29, and defining whisker geometry with base, control, and tip points swept into thin tapered tubes.

Building the torso loft...

Still defining head geometry and fur coloring...

For the snout, I'm sweeping a tapered tube along a curved path of points using a radius function that shrinks over the length, capped flat at the base and rounded at the tip.

Still writing sweep points...

I'm placing a small sphere for the nose slightly forward of the snout tip, positioning it to protrude just past the jaw's end point. I'm deciding to skip adding mouth interior geometry for now, then starting to set up eye decals using an animated eye texture generator with an amber iris.

Now I'm figuring out the decal placement logic — sampling points around the skull surface for each eye, mirroring the texture for the left side, and confirming that eyelash flicks point toward the outer corners correctly based on which side is being drawn. I'm also starting to sketch out an SVG teardrop shape for a forehead decal.

Now checking the forehead crescent mark placement against the ear positions — I need to verify the crescent's x-span doesn't overlap into the inner ear geometry, since the gap between ears is tight.

I'm shrinking the crescent radius and widening the ear base spacing to avoid overlap, then moving on to adding decorative tufts and cards on the cheeks using scatter-based placement filtered by surface normal and position.

I need the filters to exclude the eye region so scattered cards don't obstruct the eye decals, restricting placement to the sides and back of the head using normal and z-position thresholds. Next I'm setting up the chest ruff scatter on the torso surface...

Writing scatter config...

Still writing scatter and card setup...

Ring options confirm the radius placement around the tail's centerline works as expected. I'm now working out floating orb and flame positions, trying to space them so they don't overlap the tail fan while staying visible from the front.

Drawing the magic circle floor design...

Placing the circle decal just above the floor so it faces upward and glows correctly, with the axis orientation symmetric enough that star rotation doesn't matter. I'm double-checking the decal binds to the nearest bone (pelvis) and that most other colors just reuse the existing paint constants.

Now I'm building the leg loops for both sides, computing shoulder/hip points and constructing front leg chains using polyline paths passed directly as point arrays — letting `chain` smooth the corners rather than using sharp polyline joints. For parenting, I'm figuring out which spine joint is closest to the shoulder point near the front legs, landing on spine2 rather than spine3.

Hind legs parent to the pelvis, and I'm naming the joints per limb — shoulder/elbow/wrist for front, hip/knee/hock/foot for hind — matching the number of points returned by the limb function, then setting appropriate radii tapering from thicker proximal segments to thinner distal ones for each leg type.

I'm placing paw joints at the end of each leg chain, adding a haunch sphere scaled and positioned on the hind leg's hip joint, and painting it cream, then sizing anklet ring torus details based on the leg radius at a given point along the chain.

Now I'm positioning gold anklet rings on the front and hind legs where their sock markings end, computing the y-height and radius at those path points, then orienting each torus using the path's tangent vector.

I'm also setting up leg sweeps with tapered radius arrays and rounded foot caps, placing hind paw spheres relative to the foot target positions, and adjusting the flame glow intensity to 1.3.

For the dorsal flame mane, I'm computing frames along the torso spine using weighted sweep points, sizing the flame cards and flow direction for the mane, and finishing the spine ridge near the tail. I'm also checking that the body paint function returns the right color, then considering whether to add subtle ink outlines or fur-edge accents to the coat.

I'm double-checking color definitions like gold, pink, nose, plum, red, cream, and belly tones along with texture references for the tuft, shide, flame, and circle elements, making sure variables like lerp, rng, and the degree/ink constants are all actually used. Now I'm writing the neck rope code, computing a surface point on the torso and a lerped position between two reference points to anchor the shimenawa ring.

Writing the sweep and shide code...

Adjusting spacing to 14 with front-filtering down to about 6 cards, then setting up the shide card styling and starting on the tassel and bell hit logic...

I need to double check the tassel hang depth against the chest surface position so it doesn't float unrealistically in front of the body.

Now I'm lowering the rope attachment point and moving on to add a ribbon and sash with a loop that stacks a few z-depth layers.

I also want the tail flames glowing, and need to confirm front legs map to the "L" side by their x-coordinate while the hind thigh bone comes from the joint array. I'm writing a small helper that throws a descriptive error when a surface hit is missing, then using it alongside `around(center)` for positioning and building a Catmull curve from the collected hit points for the kumadori marking.
